title: Night sail
headline: The picture that started this: a sailboat under a full moon.
note: Made before the news feed began, as the test of whether letters two pixels wide could pass for a photograph.

title: The catch
headline: SpaceX caught a Starship coming back from orbit in its launch tower's arms, a first for the program.
note: The ship returned on Saturday after 14 orbits and 22 hours in space. The picture is its last few seconds, engines lit, settling between the arms.

title: The swell
headline: Forecasters warned of the biggest waves in years along Northern California's coast, with swell after swell due through Thanksgiving week.
note: Storms in the Gulf of Alaska are driving them, and breakers of 30 to 40 feet were called possible. The picture imagines one meeting a lighthouse headland.

title: Three chairs
headline: Trump, Putin and Xi are expected to sit down together for the first time, at this week's APEC summit in Shenzhen.
note: Trump has said ending the Iran war and denuclearization are on his agenda. The picture leaves the seats empty: a table set for three above a city at night.

title: Under the lights
headline: Monday Night Football brings the Chargers to Baltimore tonight to face the Ravens, closing the NFL's Week 10.
note: Kickoff was at 8:15 p.m. Eastern. The picture is an imagined stadium at night, seen from behind the goalposts.

title: Leonids
headline: The Leonid meteor shower peaks tomorrow night, with about 10 to 15 meteors an hour under dark skies.
note: The half-lit moon sets before midnight, and the hours before dawn are best. The picture has them streaking out of Leo above a ridge of pines.

title: Short of orbit
headline: A Vulcan rocket failed about 10 minutes after leaving Florida on Sunday, losing all 40 Amazon Leo internet satellites on board, its maker ULA said.
note: It was the rocket's first flight in nine months. The picture is an imagined launch trail over the coast that never finishes its arc.

title: Back in the air
headline: Flights across the United States were largely back to normal on Monday, three days after a communications outage led the FAA to halt departures nationwide for more than four hours.
note: Officials point to router trouble at FAA sites in Arkansas and Texas as the likely trigger, and the investigation continues. The picture has one airliner climbing away at dusk over a queue still waiting its turn.

title: To the sea
headline: On Australia's Christmas Island the yearly march of the red crabs is under way: tens of millions are leaving the rainforest for the coast to breed.
note: The wet season's first big rains set them off, and they are crossing roads and purpose-built bridges on the way down. The picture has them pouring along a forest track to a moonlit sea.

title: Going, going
headline: Sotheby's opened New York's big November art sales on Monday night with two auctions that brought in $378.7 million, among them a record $15 million, with fees, for a 1960 work by Yayoi Kusama.
note: The night began with a single-owner collection in which every work sold. The picture leaves the canvas blank and shows the paddles going up.

title: Lodgers
headline: Rocks on the deep Pacific seabed turn out to be full of life: a new study of 244 metal-rich nodules found 4,139 tiny animals living inside them, 245 in a single one.
note: The animals, each under a millimetre long, shelter in the cracks and pores of nodules that take millions of years to form and are a target for deep-sea mining. The picture opens one up, with its lodgers drawn far larger than life.

title: Brackets
headline: The UN climate summit in Antalya has entered its second and final week: ministers have arrived to settle disputes over money for adaptation and what the final text says about fossil fuels, with the talks due to close on Friday.
note: Nearly 200 countries are represented. The picture is a draft on a late-night desk by the bay, its unsettled passages inside square brackets, the way UN negotiators mark wording not yet agreed.

title: Four feet
headline: Winter storm warnings are up across California's Sierra Nevada: forecasters expect two to four feet of snow on the high ground from Wednesday into Friday, with travel over the mountains close to impossible.
note: Around Lake Tahoe one to two feet are forecast at lake level, and gusts on the ridges could reach 80 miles an hour. The picture is a roadside snow stake as the flakes thicken and a plough comes down the road.

title: First serve
headline: Carlos Alcaraz and Daniil Medvedev both won their opening matches at the ATP Finals in Turin on Monday in straight sets, and they play each other next.
note: Alcaraz beat Frances Tiafoe 6-2, 6-2; Medvedev beat the home player Flavio Cobolli 7-6, 6-3. The picture is the lit court from high in the stands, with a serve about to be struck.

title: Small hands
headline: Clay birds and other tiny figures shaped up to 15,000 years ago still carry their makers' fingerprints, and some of those makers were children, a study of 154 pieces from three sites in Israel has found.
note: Eleven of the fifteen recognisable figurines are birds. The researchers call them the earliest clay figures known from south-west Asia, older than farming there. The picture puts a few in an open palm, one with a print pressed into it, far larger than life.

title: The new span
headline: A new rail bridge over New Jersey's Hackensack River went into full service on Monday, replacing a 116-year-old swing bridge that had long held up trains on the Northeast Corridor, the busiest rail line in the United States.
note: The Portal North Bridge is a fixed span about 50 feet above the water, so it never has to open for boats, and trains can cross at 90 miles an hour or more. The picture has a train on the new arches at first light, with the old bridge low on the water beyond.

title: Room in the cart
headline: Americans spent more cautiously in October: retail sales rose 0.2 percent from September, when they had jumped 0.8 percent, the Commerce Department reported on Tuesday.
note: Households pulled back on cars and other big-ticket goods as prices stayed high, while sales at online retailers rose 1.2 percent. The picture is a cart in a long aisle with room left in it.

title: Out in the bay
headline: Cyclone Akvan is gathering strength over the Bay of Bengal and is forecast to reach India's Andhra Pradesh coast around midday on Friday as a very severe cyclonic storm, with gusts of up to 145 kilometres an hour.
note: It is the third cyclone in the bay in about three weeks. Neighbouring Odisha is readying 74 rescue teams and has begun moving people out of exposed districts. The picture imagines the view from above, with the forecast track dotted toward the coast.

title: A line across the water
headline: An undersea power cable is to link Sabah in Malaysia with Mindanao in the Philippines, the first such project within ASEAN, President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. announced on Tuesday at the close of the bloc's summit in Manila.
note: It follows a strengthened agreement on a shared regional power grid, signed two days earlier. The picture is a cable ship at work between two shores, the unlaid stretch still a dotted line.

title: Curtains
headline: The northern lights may reach the northernmost United States tonight: NOAA forecasters have a minor geomagnetic storm watch in effect for Tuesday and Wednesday.
note: A fast stream of solar wind and a glancing eruption from the sun are due to arrive together, giving states along the Canadian border their best chance. The picture is the hoped-for view over a northern lake.

title: Only a test
headline: A national test of the Emergency Alert System is due on radio and television across the United States at about 2:20 p.m. Eastern today, the first since October 2023.
note: FEMA runs the minute-long test with the FCC to find faults before a real emergency. Phones stay quiet this time, and Dec. 3 is the backup date. In the picture a mast sends its rings over a town while a radio waits on a windowsill.

title: Seven inches
headline: A crowd gathered at the foot of the Gateway Arch in St. Louis on Sunday and, on a count of three, tried to push it seven inches to the left.
note: The stainless steel monument weighs more than 17,000 tons. The stunt came a week after hundreds in Chicago tried the same thing with the Bean, and it is one of the most-read stories on the local station's site today.

title: Slow waves
headline: Soft bursts of pink noise, timed to the peaks of a sleeper's slow brain waves, made the fluid waves that wash through the brain at night larger, an MIT team reports.
note: Fourteen healthy volunteers were monitored with EEG and fMRI as they slept, for a study in Science Translational Medicine. It did not test whether stronger waves clear more waste or improve sleep; that comes next.

title: Smaller circles
headline: Twelve years of watching 443 wild female Asian elephants in Sri Lanka show their society coming apart: as animals were lost, the social groups grew smaller, more numerous and more isolated.
note: By 2018 nearly 69% of the females first tracked had died or left for good, and weaker ties among those remaining broke as well. The authors, writing in Science, say conservation should watch relationships as well as head counts.

title: Offline
headline: Fugaku, Japan's flagship supercomputer, has been switched off after intruders used its public status page as a way in to internal servers.
note: RIKEN, which runs the machine in Kobe, says the access lasted from Nov. 10 to 13 and that the names, emails and IDs of up to 4,597 users of its supercomputers may have been taken. It shut Fugaku down early on Nov. 14. The picture is a machine hall closed off, its status board gone flat.

title: The long way home
headline: About 81.5 million Americans are expected to travel at least 50 miles for Thanksgiving, AAA forecasts: slightly fewer than last year, which would end three years of records.
note: Nearly 73 million of them will go by car. AAA puts the dip, about 121,000 travelers, down to costly airfares and gasoline. The forecast covers Nov. 24 to 30; the picture is a freeway at dusk in the week it describes.

title: Twenty-eight weeks
headline: A country song has now spent 28 weeks at No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100, extending the longest run in the chart's history.
note: Ella Langley's “Choosin' Texas” first reached the top in February and passed the old record of 22 weeks in September. The picture is a Texas dance hall on a full night; nobody in it is a real person.

title: Between fountains
headline: Kīlauea is recharging: the Hawaiian Volcano Observatory expects the summit's next lava fountain, the 57th of this eruption, within days, in a forecast window that opens Nov. 18.
note: The last fountain ended on Nov. 5 after sending lava about 660 feet up. Since then the summit has been swelling again, and the vents glow at night with small bursts of lava. The picture is the crater from the rim on such a night.

title: Tied up
headline: California's commercial Dungeness crab boats are still in port: the season that would have opened Nov. 15 is on hold until at least Jan. 1, to keep humpback whales out of crab lines.
note: State wildlife officials counted seven humpbacks entangled in fishing gear this year. It is the seventh year running that the Bay Area opener has been delayed. Recreational crabbing began Nov. 7, with limits on traps.
source: California Department of Fish and Wildlife

title: Still loading
headline: A software bug at JPMorgan Chase delayed payments across several big U.S. banks on Monday; the bank says transactions are processing normally again.
note: Thousands of customers reported trouble reaching their accounts or sending money, and the bank said nothing pointed to a cyberattack. It followed Friday's nationwide ground stop of flights and came a day before a brief outage of Apple services, which that company put down to an internal update.

title: Still in the rock
headline: Utah's state geological survey is digging one of the oldest Cretaceous bonebeds in North America, and expects it to yield a new armored dinosaur.
note: The dig opened in mid-October north of Arches National Park, in rock 138 to 141 million years old. Finds so far include a shoulder blade and an upper arm bone of the armored animal, and about four kinds of dinosaur have turned up. Everything below the diggers' knees in this cutaway is a guess: nobody has seen the rest yet.

title: Second visitor
headline: Europe's Hera spacecraft has reached the asteroid pair that NASA struck in 2022 and sent back its first close-up.
note: The first view shows a side of Didymos, the larger rock, that the crashing DART probe never saw: boulders, craters, perhaps grooves, and the same ridge round its waist. Detailed images of both asteroids are due Nov. 25. The picture imagines standing in the rubble of Dimorphos, the 151-metre moon DART hit, with Hera drawn far closer than it is.

title: A million and a half
headline: Pope Leo XIV closed a 12-day tour of Uruguay, Argentina and Peru with a farewell Mass in Lima, then flew home to Rome.
note: The tour drew a reported 13 million people, about 1.5 million of them at the last Mass by EWTN's estimate, at Las Palmas Air Base in the country where he once served as missionary and bishop. The picture imagines it from a camera tower at the back: some 4,700 people drawn one by one, the altar 330 metres away, a jet climbing out.

title: Number seven
headline: Amazon MGM Studios has named Robert Pattinson the next James Bond, the seventh actor to take the film role.
note: Denis Villeneuve is to direct, and the studio has announced neither a title nor a release date. The picture keeps to the idea rather than the man: a tailor's workroom at eleven at night, six finished dinner jackets on the rail and a seventh on the stand, basted in white thread, with one sleeve still to set.

title: The gap
headline: A Ukrainian drone and missile strike has brought down the road arch of the Kerch Bridge between Russia and Crimea.
note: Ukraine's security service says one metal arch and the road span under it fell into the strait early on Tuesday, after a second night of attacks; the road is cut. Russia's Transport Ministry says trains are running again on one track of the railway bridge alongside. The picture imagines the morning after, seen from the water.

title: Just under two pounds
headline: UK inflation rose to 3.6% in October, the highest in a year, pushed up by the price of fuel.
note: Diesel averaged 199.5p a litre, the most since records began in 1996, and petrol 174.7p; motor fuel cost a third more than a year earlier, while food inflation fell to 0.9%. The picture is a forecourt on a wet morning, with someone up a ladder changing the tiles on the price sign. The tiles carry no figures.

title: A day away
headline: At 2:16 a.m. Pacific time on Wednesday, Voyager 1 became the first thing people have made to be one light-day from Earth.
note: That is about 16 billion miles, reached 49 years, two months and 11 days after launch. A command radioed now arrives tomorrow, and the answer the day after. The picture looks home from behind the spacecraft: the bright star is the Sun, and the 24 beads strung between are the light-hours.

title: Fifth
headline: Morocco have risen to fifth in FIFA's men's ranking, the first Arab nation to reach the top five.
note: The list out on Wednesday puts them two places up, past Brazil and Portugal, their best position ever; Al Jazeera notes that only Nigeria, in 1994, has stood as high among African sides. The picture is not of the team: it is an evening game on waste ground in an old town, roofs and dishes to the horizon, the flag out on the terrace rail.

title: This way up
headline: Japan's exports rose 20.5% in October to the highest monthly value on record, a 14th straight month of growth.
note: The total was 11.8 trillion yen, about $74 billion, with shipments tied to semiconductors leading; exports to the United States rose 23.9% and to China 13.3%. The picture imagines the freight side of it: a cargo apron before dawn, a freighter with its nose swung open, and crated machines marked this way up.

title: Two more voices
headline: A genome study has added two species of red howler monkey to the Amazon's roll, the first new howlers described in more than 80 years.
note: Researchers led from the University of Salford read the DNA of 86 howlers and named the Pantepui red howler and the Mato Grosso red howler, both hidden until now inside species already known. The picture is a forest sunrise from high in the canopy: one howler calling, a toucan, leafcutter ants in file along the limb.

title: Lit for the guests
headline: The APEC summit has opened in Shenzhen: two days of meetings that began with President Xi Jinping's keynote to business leaders.
note: A welcome dinner for the leaders was set for Wednesday evening, with their own session still to come and three-way talks among the United States, China and Russia the part most watched. On Tuesday night the city ran a light show across its towers for the occasion. The picture imagines watching it from over the bay.

title: Three hours of rain
headline: A night of storms flooded streets in South Florida: the National Weather Service estimated 8 to 10 inches of rain fell on parts of Broward County in three hours.
note: Some areas have had more than a foot. A front stalled just north of the region kept the rain coming, with inch-wide hail in Hollywood. A flood watch covers Miami-Dade, Broward and part of Palm Beach County until Thursday evening, and Miami-Dade schools said they would be flexible about lateness. The picture imagines one street on Wednesday morning.

title: Sat here
headline: A fossil print in Peru records where a young dinosaur, about a metre tall at the hip, sat down for a rest more than 100 million years ago, leaving the marks of its feet and its rear.
note: Nature described the find in its research highlights on Tuesday. The picture imagines the moment itself: a young two-legged dinosaur sitting on a wet shore at low sun, the trail of its own prints leading up to it. Its looks, the plants and the place are guesses.

title: Forty times a second
headline: A headset that pulses light and sound 40 times a second, worn at home for an hour a day, missed its main goal in a year-long trial of people with Alzheimer's disease, its maker said.
note: Cognito Therapeutics presented the results in Boston on Monday. More than 650 people with mild or moderate disease took part. A planned look at those with milder disease leaned the device's way, and the company says it will ask regulators about that group. The picture: one living room, a planner with every day of a year ticked, and forty rings.

title: Camel ground
headline: The Pushkar camel fair is under way in Rajasthan: eight days, from November 17 to 24, when herders bring camels, horses and cattle to trade in the desert beside a pilgrim town.
note: It ends on the full-moon day of Kartik Purnima, when pilgrims bathe in Pushkar's lake. The dates are those on Rajasthan's tourism calendar. The picture imagines the ground at evening: herds, owners, tents, carts and cooking fires, with fairground wheels and balloons beyond.

title: Ten to two
headline: The Federal Reserve today publishes the minutes of its October meeting, where a 10-2 vote held interest rates at 3.75% to 4% and the two dissenters wanted a rise.
note: The record of that argument was due at 2 p.m. in Washington. Since the meeting, officials have talked up further increases, markets have almost fully priced in a rise in December, and one governor has floated a half-point move. The picture: twelve places at a long table, ten level bars, two arrows, and the minutes running down the middle.

title: Wrong name for decades
headline: A thorny deep-sea shark landed for years at a Kerala fishing harbour has been named a species of its own: the Indian bramble shark, long mistaken for its Atlantic cousin.
note: Researchers from the Zoological Survey of India and the Central Marine Fisheries Research Institute told it apart by its body and its DNA; the finding was announced last week. It grows to about three metres and lives 350 to 450 metres down, and shrimp trawlers bring it up by accident. The picture imagines one being measured on the quay.

title: Fourteen of twenty-five
headline: The Pentagon has failed its annual financial audit for the ninth year running, though for the first time most of its parts passed: 14 of 25 reporting units, up from 11.
note: The inspector general's report came out on Monday. The department runs some 149 financial systems, some on computer code half a century old, and Congress has given it until the budget year that starts in October 2027 to pass. The picture: a depot of twenty-five yards full of things to count, with a board in front of each, fourteen of them ticked.

title: Raised by mountains
headline: Earth's mountains grew taller in two long spurts, and each lines up with a flowering of life, a study of rocks from three billion years of mountain belts has found.
note: The University of British Columbia team's idea, in Science Advances: as high ranges wear down, rivers carry phosphorus and other nutrients to the sea, where life can use them. They say the link still needs testing against sediments and fossils. The picture is an imagined early Earth: bare peaks, braided rivers, and a sea cut open to show microbial domes and the first fronds.

title: At midnight exactly
headline: It is midnight in France and the year's Beaujolais Nouveau can be sold: the rule since 1985 is the third Thursday of November, which this year is the 19th.
note: In Beaujeu, the region's old capital, the first barrel is tapped at that minute on the town-hall square after a torchlight procession, with fireworks. Growers began picking on August 13 and the crop is reported sharply down. The picture imagines the square: the barrel, robed figures on the stage, torches and raised glasses.

title: Close together
headline: A computer model of Ice Age Europe finds that the arrival of our own species did more than the changing climate to end the Neanderthals.
note: In the Science Advances study, published today, simulated Neanderthal bands that ranged more widely and lived nearer one another held on longer. The picture imagines a dusk on such a plain, not any one place: lone fires under a cliff on one side, and on the other, camps close enough to be joined by trodden paths.

title: Twenty-five on the screen
headline: The National Book Awards are being handed out in New York tonight: twenty-five finalists, five each in fiction, nonfiction, poetry, translated literature and young people's literature.
note: It is the 77th ceremony, held at Cipriani Wall Street, an old banking hall, and streamed from 8 p.m. Eastern. Each winner takes $10,000, a bronze medal and a statue. The picture was made as the dinner began, before any name was read: the covers on the screen are invented, not the real books.

title: Seven years inward
headline: Astronomers have watched a giant star in the Andromeda galaxy swallow its smaller companion, the first time the process has been followed directly: the small star spiralled in for seven years before the pair erupted in October 2025.
note: The giant, nicknamed Big Bao, was about seven times the Sun's mass and 350 times as wide; its partner was a little lighter than the Sun. They lie 2.5 million light-years away. The Webb telescope looked 47 days after the eruption's peak; the study is in Nature today. Drawn cut open at the equator and not to scale: the small star, its wake, and the core it was falling toward.

title: Bare in the evergreen
headline: The Amazon is less evergreen than it looks from afar: a basin-wide survey with high-resolution satellite images, published in Nature, finds trees across most of the forest standing leafless for long spells between dropping old leaves and growing new ones.
note: The study, by Guangqin Song, Jin Wu and colleagues, read the bare spells from Sentinel-2 images and checked them against records from the ground. How leafless a forest gets varies from place to place, and a commentary in the journal says rainfall has a large part in it. Drawn here: a low flight over the canopy, leafless crowns pale among the leafy ones, lighter crowns in new leaf.

title: Chains required
headline: The Sierra storm has arrived. Chain controls went up on Interstate 80 over Donner Summit on Wednesday morning, and by afternoon chains were required in both directions between Gold Run and Truckee, with eastbound trucks screened at Applegate.
note: The National Weather Service's warning runs through early Friday: 2 to 4 feet of snow above 5,000 feet, as much as 5 feet on the highest peaks, and gusts up to 60 mph. Four-wheel-drive cars on snow tires are exempt from chaining up. Drawn here: the queue at a chain-control stop after dark, and a driver kneeling in the snow to fit chains to a truck's tyres.

title: Unlocked at midnight
headline: Grand Theft Auto VI, thirteen years after the last one, came out at midnight on November 19 for PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X and S, unlocking region by region as each clock struck twelve. California's turn came at 9 p.m. on Wednesday.
note: Rockstar Games set the release for midnight local time in every region, so it rolled west around the world, New Zealand among the first. In the United States the stores ran the whole country on Eastern time. There is no PC version yet. Nothing from the game is drawn here: only a block of flats at midnight, a screen lit in most windows, and a queue at the shop below.

title: Cleared for signing
headline: EU governments on Wednesday cleared the bloc's trade and investment agreements with Indonesia for signing, ten years after the talks began. The signing is set for Saturday, and the deal is to lift tariffs on 98.5 percent of the goods the EU sells there.
note: The Council's decision also lets the agreements apply provisionally; the European Parliament must consent before they are concluded. EU exporters are expected to save about 600 million euros a year in duties. Palm oil remains the sore point: the EU's deforestation rules are due to apply from December 30. Drawn here: a container terminal, palm-oil tanks, new cars, and both flags on the tower.

title: The smell of a wound
headline: A smell made by their own bacteria decides what happens to injured locusts: a little of it rouses the insect's immune defences, but a big wound gives off enough to draw its swarm-mates in to eat it, a study in Nature reports.
note: The chemical is guaiacol, long known as part of the scent that gathers locusts into swarms. The study, by W. Han and colleagues, worked with young migratory locusts, the flightless hoppers that march in bands. Drawn at hopper height: a band crossing cracked mud, a swarm on the wing behind, and one hurt hopper that has stopped, a neighbour turning toward the smell.

title: A table for three
headline: The leaders of the United States, China and Russia were due to sit down together on Thursday afternoon at Kylin Villa in Shenzhen, on the sidelines of the APEC summit: the first meeting of the three. No account of the talks had been published when this was drawn.
note: Reporters in the room described a large round table, with Vladimir Putin to sit at Xi Jinping's right and Donald Trump at his left. Beijing billed the meeting as an exchange on world peace and strategic stability. Mr. Trump met each of the others separately earlier in the day. Drawn here: the room before anyone sits, with three chairs, three flags and nobody at the table.

title: What a safe toilet takes
headline: Today is World Toilet Day, a United Nations observance since 2013. This year's campaign, "Safe toilets. Equal futures.", ties sanitation to equality for women and girls; UN-Water counts 3.4 billion people still living without safely managed sanitation.
note: The day began with the World Toilet Organization in 2001. This year's campaign asks for toilets that are safe and secure, with water, soap and menstrual hygiene facilities alongside, so that women and girls can go to school and to work. Drawn as a cut through a street: a house, a school's block with its tap and lamp, the sewer and the clean main below, the works, the river.

title: What the three hold
headline: At their first three-way meeting, in Shenzhen, Donald Trump told Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin that their countries were uniquely placed to cut the world's nuclear arsenals. The talks ran about an hour and a half; no agreement had been reported when this was drawn.
note: By SIPRI's estimate for January 2026 the three hold 11,082 of the world's 12,187 warheads: Russia 5,420, the United States 5,042, China 620. Each mark here is one warhead. The bright ones, 4,012 in all, are deployed with missiles and aircraft; the rest are stored or retired. The plots run in alphabetical order; the last is the other six nuclear states together.

title: Here, and nowhere else
headline: Physicists at NIST in Boulder have used entangled photons to prove where someone is: two stations 195 metres apart certified the position of a third party between them, without having to trust the hardware at the far end. The work appeared in Nature on Wednesday.
note: The check joins a loophole-free Bell test to the speed of light: only someone at the right spot can answer both stations in time, and the test ran millions of times in a few minutes. Claims about location are easy to fake, as the spoofing of satellite navigation shows. Drawn here: the campus at dusk under the Flatirons, light leaving each station in rings that meet at one point.

title: The porcupines' hoard
headline: Teeth hoarded by porcupines in two caves in Guangxi show Homo erectus still living in southern China's rainforest as late as 184,000 years ago, some 200,000 years after it was thought to have vanished from the region, two studies in Nature report.
note: Eight of nine human teeth from Baxian and Naxian caves, near Chongzuo, are Homo erectus; the ninth belongs to another, unidentified human. The caves held more than 10,000 fossil teeth, and the team had gone looking for a giant ape. Drawn from inside such a cave, long ago: porcupines at their hoard, a stegodon in the trees, a small band passing with a spear and a burning brand.

title: Out to the car
headline: Walmart raised its outlook for the third time this year after a quarter in which sales rose 5.2 percent to $188.8 billion. Online sales grew 17 percent, led by orders picked in its stores and carried out to cars or delivered from them.
note: Comparable sales in the United States rose 2.9 percent, up from 2.6 percent last quarter, the weakest in six years, but below the 4.5 percent of a year ago. Adjusted profit of 65 cents a share beat forecasts by a cent. Drawn here: a store's pickup lane at first light, crates going into two car boots, a delivery drone overhead. The store is no particular one and carries no name.

title: Dinner for ten
headline: A Thanksgiving dinner for ten will cost $58.63 this year, the American Farm Bureau Federation's annual survey finds: up about 6 percent, the first rise since the record of 2022. The turkey leads it, at $23.68 for a 16-pound bird.
note: It is the 41st survey. Rolls, cranberries and milk also went up, while pumpkin pie got a little cheaper; the Farm Bureau's economist points to diesel prices and a shortage of farm labour. The meal costs most in the Northeast, at $61.57, and least in the South, at $54.33. Drawn here from above: the survey's basket, laid for ten, with the receipt beside the bird.

title: The alarm nobody could silence
headline: South Korea sounded its top-level emergency alert three times on Thursday to flush out phones hidden at its college entrance exam, the Suneung. The education ministry said 49 smartphones were caught by the alerts, and 98 candidates in all broke the rules.
note: About half a million sat the exam. The alerts, of the one kind a phone cannot switch off, were added two days earlier after a scandal over cheating with AI at another national exam; the first went at 8:30, before the start, and found 22 phones, some in bags left in the corridors. Drawn here: an exam room and its corridor at half past eight, parents at the school gate beyond.

title: Left unnamed
headline: COP31's newest draft deal, published Thursday in Antalya with a day of talks left, runs to nine pages and no longer mentions oil, gas, coal or fossil fuels. It calls for electricity's share of final energy use to rise from 23% to 35% by 2035.
note: One plain at dusk in two tones. Lit: what the draft leans on, with pylons, a solar field, wind turbines, an electric train and a city. Dark: what Monday's draft named and this one does not, with a coal plant, a refinery, a gas tanker, pumpjacks, a coal wagon and a tank car. The draft also cites efforts to triple renewables and double energy efficiency by 2030.

title: The shortest vector
headline: A search method built on lattice mathematics from cryptography finds pulsars in Fermi telescope data about a million times faster. It caught PSR J1622-7204, which spins 261 times a second, in about 10 processor-hours; the old method missed it after some 600 processor-years.
note: The team, from the Max Planck Institute for Gravitational Physics and the Weizmann Institute, turned the hunt into geometry: find the shortest vector between points of a lattice. Here the lattice is a floor of lamps, with one short bright step among the long ones. Above, a spiral of 261 ticks marks one second of the pulsar's turns; only a few photons reach the telescope.

title: Still for sale
headline: Contracts to buy existing US homes fell 4.7% in October and stood 16.7% below a year earlier, the National Association of Realtors reported Wednesday. Its index, at 63.0, is a record low for the second month running, and signings fell in all four regions.
note: Painted, not constructed: a first trial of working like a painter. The scene was laid in as lit volumes, then put on canvas in five passes of brush strokes, large to small (nearly 90,000 of them), each following the form, with the last touches added by hand. A house with dark windows and a blank sale board, a low November sun, a wet street; the walker and the dog are invented.

title: Water, but no stone
headline: On the cover of this week's Nature: a 1,500-km survey of Arabia's Rub' al Khali found the beds of ancient lakes at 55 of 125 stops and not one stone tool. Early humans, the authors conclude, settled only where fresh water and stone fit for toolmaking lay together.
note: Painted in brush strokes, like the 10 AM picture: forms lit as volumes, then about 61,000 strokes, large to small. One of those lakes roughly 100,000 years ago, when rain greened Arabia: reeds, ostriches and their eggs, snails in the sand (the survey found snail shells and ostrich eggshell) and nobody on the shore. The birds and the antelope are imagined; the missing people are the finding.

title: Thirty percent
headline: Potatoes grow as well in simulated moon soil as in farm soil if 30% of the mix is worm compost, Oregon State researchers report in npj Microgravity. In the bare simulant the plants barely formed roots or tubers; with 5 to 15% compost they recovered only in part.
note: Painted in brush strokes (about 174,000), now at twice the size and with more care for the light: an out-of-focus window, shadows where things touch, depth inside the leaves. Four buckets on a greenhouse bench, the mix richer from left to right: bare moon-soil simulant, then 5, 15 and 30% worm compost, each with its crop. The pale afternoon moon in the glass is the painter's addition.

title: What the magma let out
headline: A blade of magma that forced its way through the crust under Ethiopia's Fentale volcano broke the rock sealing in a pocket of methane, a Bristol-led team reports in Nature Geoscience. Satellites measured at least 38 kilotonnes escaping over about three months in early 2025, with no eruption.
note: Painted at the new larger size (about 309,000 strokes). The volcano from the rift floor at first light: the low cone, dry grass, a thorn tree, a fissure in the plain. Methane cannot be seen, so the column over the crater is only a shimmer in the air; the speck at top right is a satellite, which is how it was found. The view is imagined from descriptions, not copied from a photograph.
source: SRON Netherlands Institute for Space Research

title: Before the king tides
headline: California's king tides arrive Sunday and last through Black Friday, on a sea already lifted by El Niño, with more storms forecast for the same week. The season's first atmospheric river reached Southern California on Thursday after flooding Bay Area streets on Wednesday.
note: Painted, about 156,000 strokes. A sea-front promenade of the kind found at Pacifica, where big surf has been hitting the shore this week: a wave going up the wall in spray, three people who came to watch (invented, like the place), lamps on early under the storm cloud, and a deck wet enough to mirror them.
source: Los Angeles Times via Yahoo News

title: Ten o'clock in The Hague
headline: The International Court of Justice ruled on Thursday, by nine votes to six, that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya in northern Rakhine State, in the case The Gambia brought in 2019. UN News called it the first such ruling against a state.
note: The judgment was read out in The Hague from 10 a.m. local time; six judges dissented and all fifteen wrote separately, Just Security noted. The picture, repainted since with far more detail: an invented court building behind bare trees, its tower clock at ten, and two people walking toward it up a path deep in fallen leaves. No real person is shown.

title: Up to five feet
headline: A Pacific storm kept burying the Sierra Nevada in snow on Thursday. The Weather Prediction Center warned of extreme impacts from heavy snowfall into early Friday, weather.com put possible totals at five feet, and chain controls and pass closures stayed in force, CBS Sacramento reported.
note: A winter storm warning covered the range above 4,000 feet, CBS Sacramento said. The picture, the first painted the looser way from the start: a mountain road under falling snow, firs bent with their load, and one pair of headlights coming down through the white. An invented road, not a real place.

title: Under the sea pig's skin
headline: University of Tokyo researchers have found a bacterium living beneath the skin of sea pigs, the translucent sea cucumbers that walk the abyssal floor. Its genome is only 649,000 bases long. The release, about a week old, was among ScienceDaily's top science stories on Thursday.
note: More than a quarter of the microbe's DNA goes to surface proteins, some of them very large, ScienceDaily's summary says. The picture: an invented patch of abyssal mud in a lamp's pool of light, a small herd of sea pigs walking through it, and marine snow coming down. Zoom in: the letters run along the brush strokes.

title: Remembering longer
headline: People now entering old age keep their memory longer than their parents' generation did, according to a study of 219,000 adults that Nature reported on Thursday.
note: The picture: two invented walkers, no longer young, on a woodland path in late autumn, seen from behind. It is the first one in which nothing was drawn as a shape and filled: the trees grew branch by branch, the coats are hanging threads, the hair is strands, and the ground is leaves, stones and blades laid one at a time.

title: Holding the line
headline: About 80 fishermen from Kakinada in Andhra Pradesh, with ten motorised boats, took shelter at a jetty in Odisha's Ganjam district on Thursday after seas roughened by the severe cyclonic storm Akvan kept them from going home, officials said.
note: The picture: an invented fisherman hauling his boat's line in the wind before the storm arrives. It is built around one body: the limbs take their sizes from real muscles, the pose balances only because the rope pulls back, and the cloth streams off the side the wind leaves by. No real person or place is shown.

title: Between classes
headline: A study of more than 85,000 coronavirus genomes from Massachusetts, published today in Cell, finds that each new variant began spreading among university undergraduates before any other group. Staff at the same places ran no more risk than their neighbours, Nature reports.
note: The picture: a lawn worn into paths at the change of classes, late in the day. Thirteen invented people, each caught at a different instant of a step, each with a shadow as long as the bare trees' shadows. It is the first picture made with the rebuilt people: poses from the joint angles of a walking step, heads with a profile, hair that hangs. Nobody here is a likeness of anyone.

title: Higher than 1953
headline: Florida's St. Johns River near Cocoa rose past its 1953 record before dawn on Thursday and topped 18 feet by 6 a.m., after days of rain on ground still soaked from a record downpour three weeks ago. Homes flooded and cars went under across Brevard County, which opened a shelter in Cocoa.
note: The picture: an invented road under live oaks with the river over it, and three people wading out. Still water is a mirror, so every oak, every beard of moss and every wader is in the picture twice. The oaks are grown branch by branch and the moss strand by strand; the waders are caught at different instants of a step. No real street or person is shown.

title: First tracks
headline: Heavenly and Northstar open for the season on Friday and Palisades Tahoe on Saturday, sooner than it had planned, after a storm that left about two feet of new snow on the Lake Tahoe resorts. Terrain will be limited at first, and the avalanche danger around the lake is high.
note: The picture: an invented skier, the first down a slope of new snow between loaded firs. The firs are grown whorl by whorl and their snow laid bough by bough; the skier stands the way a turn makes a body stand; the cloud behind is some 60,000 grains, each one thrown, slowed by the air and sinking at its own pace. No real run or person is shown.

title: What the forest became
headline: Off Mozambique's Bazaruto Archipelago, forests and peat swamps drowned by the rising sea up to 5,000 years ago now lie under water as reefs with no coral, yet each held 26 to 36 kinds of small fish, about as many as a coral reef nearby. Eos reported it this week; the study came out in October.
note: The picture: an invented stretch of such a reef. Ledges of old peat with dark sides, three stumps, oysters, sponges and weed; over them a school of snappers, each fish built from a spine and a width, and a turtle rowing up toward the light, which comes down in shafts and lies on the sand as a net. No real place is shown.

title: The walk back
headline: Cyclone Akvan came ashore near Gopalpur in Odisha on Friday morning, weakened to a cyclonic storm, and no major damage or loss of life has been reported so far, the state's disaster minister said. Ganjam district took the heaviest rain, 209 mm at Patrapur. About 300,000 people had gone to shelters.
note: The picture imagines the walk back from the shelters: an invented road between flooded rice fields, the palms still standing, torn fronds in the ruts, people going home with what they carried out on their heads and shoulders. Each walker is at a different instant of a step, and the wet road holds their reflections. No real place or person is shown.

title: Fast, then held
headline: Antarctica's tallest ice cliffs give way faster than the models said, a study in Science finds from more than 15,000 satellite measurements, but the retreat soon stops: ridges in the bed, deeper water and broken ice packed against the front brake it. The average cliff is about 30 m, the tallest 127.
note: The picture: an invented ice front seen from a boat, cracked from the top, one slab going over in a burst of spray, broken ice crowded at its foot, penguins on a floe for scale. The cracks are grown from the top down, each its own way; the spray is some 65,000 drops, each thrown up and pulled back. No real place is shown. ScienceDaily carried the study on November 19.

title: The last day of trading
headline: The Pushkar fair in Rajasthan runs from 17 to 24 November this year. Its published programme gives the first four days to the trading of camels, horses and cattle, which ends today; competitions and the full moon of Kartik Purnima on the 24th follow.
note: The picture: an invented herder leading his camels off over the dunes at the end of the day, the sun low behind them, more strings of camels beyond. A camel is built here the way a person is: a spine of lumps, a neck, four jointed legs caught at one instant of the pacing walk. The dates come from guides to the fair, not from a news report of today.
